package flakyprobe

import (
	"os"
	"testing"
)

// marker is how TestFlakyNew tells one process invocation from the next. The
// probe is deterministically flaky — a clock or a rand here would make the
// fixture proving the gate the gate's own first false positive.
const marker = "second-run.marker"

// TestPreExistingStable is declared at the merge-base as well as at HEAD, so
// it is not new and the gate never reruns it.
func TestPreExistingStable(t *testing.T) {
	if Sum(2, 2) != 4 {
		t.Fatal("Sum(2, 2) != 4")
	}
}

// TestDeterministicNew is new at HEAD and agrees with itself across the two
// runs, which is the whole of what the gate asks of a new test.
func TestDeterministicNew(t *testing.T) {
	if Sum(1, 2) != 3 {
		t.Fatal("Sum(1, 2) != 3")
	}
}

// TestFlakyNew is new at HEAD and disagrees with itself: it passes in the
// process that finds no marker and leaves one behind, and fails in the next
// process, which finds it.
func TestFlakyNew(t *testing.T) {
	if _, err := os.Stat(marker); err == nil {
		t.Fatal("a second process saw the marker this test left behind")
	}
	if err := os.WriteFile(marker, []byte("1"), 0o600); err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("writing the marker: %v", err)
	}
}

// TestNewSubtests is new at HEAD and names its subtests at runtime, which is
// why the top-level function is the unit the gate reruns: a report records
// `TestNewSubtests/one`, and no parse of the source can enumerate that.
func TestNewSubtests(t *testing.T) {
	for _, n := range []string{"one", "two"} {
		t.Run(n, func(t *testing.T) {
			if Sum(1, 1) != 2 {
				t.Fatal("Sum(1, 1) != 2")
			}
		})
	}
}
